rv.q: In a time of polarisation and performative outrage, this show is a hymn to tolerance and the ability to laugh with others and at oneself.
This fusillade of laser-focused facetiousness feels like the perfect piffle for our turbulent times.
It’s still a winningly funny proposition for a new generation – and Marber pulls out all the stops to raise the Garrick roof.
Patrick Marber's revival is so full of mischief that you're simply swept along by the sheer ridiculousness of it all.
Fortunately, original helmer-choreographer Susan Stroman was on hand to restore some kick and bite to the all-time biggest Tony winner, and a fine time was to be had.
The Mel Brooks classic is delivered with taste-trampling gusto
If you want non-stop giggles, gloriously provocative jokes and an easy escape from everyday misery, there's no better place to be right now than the Garrick.
Marber's new production adds enough energy and verve to sweep away the doubts.
But it’s not actually a radical reworking, and I think The Producers in 2025 probably needs that to speak to our times.
Trevor Ashley is perfectly cast as the scene-stealing director Roger De Bris…Harry Morrison also gives a stand-out performance.
And yet I cannot deny it – I left the theatre cheerfully humming the production’s earworm of a centrepiece showstopper, the crazily jaunty “Springtime for Hitler”.
I'm not sure anything new is achieved with this production, but then, that's always been the case with The Producers onstage.
All in all, this is a musical that still guarantees laugh after laugh after laugh, with a genuinely brilliant score from Brooks.
Whatever it is that was missing has certainly been found this time around, as the West End transfer is an obvious five-star show.
We roared with delight throughout at the big numbers and broad gags, and the smaller, but no less joyous or clever, delights.
Outrageous, audacious and utterly unmissable, this West End revival is a triumph of impeccable casting, razor-sharp direction and a laugh-a-minute script.
The Producers really is an outstanding collective production where every performer shows up and delivers.
Everyone has enormous fun and so, in consequence, we do too

As directed by Patrick Marber, the party scene where our devious pair attempt to cajole a pseud-director Roger Debris (Trevor Ashley) and his largely pointless camp side-kick, is particularly lacking in sophistication and resorts too often to slap-stick and lewd kitsch.
Patrick Marber's production is a sparkling, comedic masterpiece.
